This tutorial uses the National Supported Work (NSW) job-training data from
LaLonde's evaluation study and the Dehejia-Wahba data archive. It demonstrates
the full applied workflow:

1. State the causal question.
2. Hypothesize a causal graph.
3. Identify the effect from the graph.
4. Estimate the effect using `estimate_causal()`.

The outcome is real earnings in 1978. The treatment is participation in the NSW
job-training program. The data are available from Rajeev Dehejia's NBER archive:
<https://users.nber.org/~rdehejia/data/.nswdata2.html>.

## Setup

```{julia}
import Pkg
Pkg.activate(joinpath(@__DIR__, ".."); io=devnull)

using CausalGraphs
using DataFrames
using DelimitedFiles
using Downloads
using Printf
using Statistics
```

## 1. Causal question

We want the average causal effect of the job-training program on later earnings:

```text
E[re78(treat = 1)] - E[re78(treat = 0)]
```

The NSW experimental sample contains treated and control units from the same
randomized program. The variables in these text files are:

```text
treat, age, educ, black, hisp, married, nodegr, re74, re75, re78
```

where `re74`, `re75`, and `re78` are real earnings in 1974, 1975, and 1978.

```{julia}
function read_nsw_file(url)
    local_file = Downloads.download(url; timeout=120)
    x = readdlm(local_file)
    DataFrame(
        x,
        [:treat, :age, :educ, :black, :hisp, :married,
         :nodegr, :re74, :re75, :re78],
    )
end

base = "https://users.nber.org/~rdehejia/data"
treated = read_nsw_file("$base/nswre74_treated.txt")
control = read_nsw_file("$base/nswre74_control.txt")

data = vcat(treated, control)
data.u74 = Float64.(data.re74 .== 0)
data.u75 = Float64.(data.re75 .== 0)

println("n = ", nrow(data))
println("treated = ", sum(data.treat .== 1), ", controls = ", sum(data.treat .== 0))
first(data, 3)
```

## 2. Hypothesize a graph

For the randomized NSW sample, the simplest causal graph says that treatment
affects later earnings, while pre-treatment characteristics may also affect
later earnings:

```text
age, educ, race, marital status, prior earnings  ->  re78
treat                                           ->  re78
```

Because treatment was randomized within the NSW experiment, the graph does not
put arrows from pre-treatment characteristics into `treat`.

```{julia}
covars = [:age, :educ, :black, :hisp, :married, :nodegr, :re74, :re75, :u74, :u75]

graph = make_graph(
    vertices = vcat(covars, [:treat, :re78]),
    di_edges = vcat(
        [(x, :re78) for x in covars],
        [(:treat, :re78)],
    ),
)
```

This graph encodes a randomized-treatment estimand. The covariates are not
needed for confounding control, but they make the substantive assumptions
explicit and can be useful in alternative observational graphs.

## 3. Identify

`identify()` reads the graph and chooses the estimation strategy.

```{julia}
id = identify(graph, :treat, :re78)
println("strategy: ", id.strategy)
```

The effect is `:a_fixable`: no hidden or observed backdoor path from treatment
to outcome remains open in this graph. `estimate_causal()` will therefore route
to the backdoor/a-fixable estimators.

## 4. Estimate

```{julia}
res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = data,
    graph = graph,
    treatment = :treat,
    outcome = :re78,
)

@printf("TMLE:    ACE = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
        res[:TMLE].ACE, res[:TMLE].lower_ci, res[:TMLE].upper_ci)
@printf("Onestep: ACE = %.2f\n", res[:Onestep].ACE)
@printf("Gcomp:   ACE = %.2f\n", res[:Gcomp].ACE)
@printf("IPW:     ACE = %.2f\n", res[:IPW].ACE)
```

For this randomized graph, the estimators reduce to the treated-control mean
contrast. We can verify that directly:

```{julia}
raw_difference =
    mean(data.re78[data.treat .== 1]) - mean(data.re78[data.treat .== 0])

@printf("Raw treated-control difference = %.2f\n", raw_difference)
```

The graph is doing something important even in this simple case: it records why
the raw comparison has a causal interpretation.

## Observational variant

A common non-experimental version compares NSW treated units to controls drawn
from the Current Population Survey (CPS). In that setting, treatment status also
marks sample membership, so a more plausible graph includes observed
pre-treatment predictors of both treatment/sample membership and later earnings:

```text
covariates -> treat
covariates -> re78
treat      -> re78
```

That graph is still backdoor/a-fixable, but the identifying assumption is now
stronger: after conditioning on the measured covariates, there is no remaining
unmeasured confounding of treatment and earnings. The code change is only the
edge set and the control file:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
cps_controls = read_nsw_file("$base/cps3_controls.txt")
obs_data = vcat(treated, cps_controls)
obs_data.u74 = Float64.(obs_data.re74 .== 0)
obs_data.u75 = Float64.(obs_data.re75 .== 0)

obs_graph = make_graph(
    vertices = vcat(covars, [:treat, :re78]),
    di_edges = vcat(
        [(x, :treat) for x in covars],
        [(x, :re78) for x in covars],
        [(:treat, :re78)],
    ),
)

identify(obs_graph, :treat, :re78).strategy

obs_res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = obs_data,
    graph = obs_graph,
    treatment = :treat,
    outcome = :re78,
)
```

This is the usual applied workflow: the graph states the assumptions, the
identifier checks whether those assumptions are sufficient, and the estimator
computes the corresponding statistical estimand.
